title: Rome, unhindered (Acts 28:30–31)
hook: Paul under house arrest, welcoming all, preaching with confidence

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shipwreck, and every soul brought safe to Malta. Your line was not a hair shall perish.

A prisoner walks toward the capital of the world, as Luke's readers knew it. Back on day five hundred thirty-four, at the very start of Acts, Jesus told his friends they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Since then the story has gone out of the upper room, through Samaria and the desert road, to Antioch, across the sea to Philippi, Athens and Corinth, and through a shipwreck. Now it reaches Rome, and Paul walks in as a prisoner.
screen: `JERUSALEM, JUDEA, SAMARIA.` → `ANTIOCH, PHILIPPI, ATHENS.` → `AND NOW, ROME.`

segments.voice: As Paul nears the city on the Appian Way, believers from Rome walk out to meet him, at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, Luke says, he thanked God and took courage. Even an apostle needed friends to show up. In Rome he's allowed to live by himself, with a soldier guarding him. He calls together the leaders of the Jewish community and speaks with them all day, from morning to evening. Some are persuaded, some are not, and they leave still discussing among themselves. Then come the last two verses of the book, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he remained two whole years in his own hired lodging; and he received all that came in to him, Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching the things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, without prohibition." That's how Acts ends. Not with Paul's trial. Not with his death. The Douay says without prohibition; the last word in the Greek, akolutos, means unhindered, without hindrance. A man in chains, renting a room, opening his door to whoever comes, and the word is not chained. Why does Luke stop there? Nobody knows for certain. Maybe he wrote before the trial ended. Maybe he wanted the story to stay open, because it isn't finished. Catholic tradition holds that Paul was later martyred in Rome under Nero and buried on the road to Ostia, where the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls now stands. Acts itself doesn't tell it.
screen: `FRIENDS WALK OUT TO MEET HIM.` · `A ROOM, A GUARD, AN OPEN DOOR.` · `HE RECEIVED ALL THAT CAME.` · `THE BOOK ENDS OPEN.` · then, large: `WITHOUT HINDRANCE.`

segments.voice: Paul couldn't go anywhere, so he let the world come to him. Picture your own small room, your desk, your kitchen, your phone, and who might come through it: an unexpected call, a neighbor, a coworker with a question, a kid with a long story; picture receiving them the way Paul received all that came in, with the door open. If you pray, thank God for the friends who walked out to meet you when you needed it.
Rome. Where Acts ends, with Paul in a rented room, welcoming everyone, preaching without hindrance. Today's word.

Your line: without hindrance. And that's the Acts of the Apostles: witnesses, Pentecost, deacons, the road to Damascus, the council, Lydia, the jail, Athens, the shipwreck, and Rome. Tomorrow, the letters.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Saints Peter and Paul together on June 29, and pilgrims to Rome visit Paul's tomb at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, on the road to Ostia.

what a scholar hears: the last word is akōlytōs, unhindered. Paul's martyrdom comes from early tradition, not from Acts: 1 Clement speaks of it, and later writers place it under Nero.

chat.who: a friend from your book club
chat.says: How does the book of Acts end? With Paul's death?
options: No: Paul spends two years in a rented room in Rome, preaching without hindrance.
It ends with the shipwreck on Malta, before Paul ever reaches the city.
It ends with Paul back in Jerusalem, telling the elders about his journeys.
chat.meaning: Acts ends with Paul two whole years in his own hired lodging, receiving all who came and preaching without hindrance. It doesn't tell his trial or death.

Appian Way.meaning: the road Paul took into Rome

Three Taverns.meaning: a stop where believers from Rome came out to meet him

akolutos.meaning: Greek: unhindered, the very last word of Acts

Nero.meaning: the emperor under whom tradition says Paul was martyred

Ostia.meaning: Rome's port; tradition says Paul was buried on the road to it

notes: Akōlytōs as the final word of Acts: standard; confirm.
The Acts look-back in the carry names the block's main stops (days 534–558), not every day; confirm.
Paul's martyrdom under Nero, beheaded, buried on the Via Ostiensis: tradition (1 Clement 5; Eusebius); confirm framing.
The meeting with the Jewish leaders (28:17–28) is told neutrally, without making them a foil; confirm tone.
